'''Susan Landau''' (born 1954) is an American mathematician, engineer, cybersecurity policy expert, and Bridge professor in cybersecurity and policy at the [[Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy]] at [[Tufts University]].<ref name="tufts">{{cite web |title=Susan Landau |url=https://engineering.tufts.edu/people/faculty/susan-landau |access-date=April 15, 2018}} and {{cite web |title=Security and Conflict Resolution: Susan Landau |url=http://fletcher.tufts.edu/Research/Faculty-Profiles/Security-and-Conflict-Resolution/Landau |access-date=April 15, 2018}}</ref><ref name=NSA>{{cite web |url=https://uk.news.yahoo.com/cybersecurity-bill-shift-power-away-080747797.html |title=Cybersecurity Bill Would Shift Power Away From NSA |accessdate=August 28, 2017 |work=[[Yahoo! News]]}}</ref> She previously worked as a senior staff privacy analyst at [[Google]].<ref name=privacyink>{{cite web |url=http://privacyink.org/ |title=Susan Landau Biography |work=PrivacyInk |accessdate=September 6, 2013}}</ref> She was a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim fellow]]<ref name="List of Guggenheim Fellows for 2012">{{cite web |url=http://www.gf.org/news-events/2012-Fellows-in-the-United-States-and-Canada/ |title=List of Guggenheim Fellowships awarded in 2012 |access-date=September 6, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120816003220/http://www.gf.org/news-events/2012-Fellows-in-the-United-States-and-Canada |archive-date=August 16, 2012}}</ref> and a visiting scholar at the Computer Science Department, [[Harvard University]] in 2012.<ref>[http://www.linkedin.com/profile/view?id=65543255 Susan Landau] at LinkedIn</ref>

== Career ==

Landau is an alumna of [[Bronx Science]]. She then graduated with an A.B. in [[mathematics]] from [[Princeton University]] in 1976 after completing a senior thesis titled "Simple algebras", under the supervision of [[John Coleman Moore]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Landau |first=Susan |url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/3708076 |title=Simple algebras |date=1976 |publisher=Princeton, NJ: Department of Mathematics |language=English}}</ref> She went on to receive a master's degree from [[Cornell University]] in 1979 before pursuing graduate studies at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where she received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in mathematics in 1983 after completing a doctoral dissertation, titled "On computing [[Galois group]]s and its application to solvability by radicals", under the supervision of [[Gary Miller (computer scientist)|Gary L. Miller]].<ref name="tufts"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Landau |first=Susan |date= |title=On computing Galois groups and its application to solvability by radicals |url=http://library.mit.edu/F/?func=find-b&find_code=SYS&local_base=mit01pub&request=000202723 |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date=June 22, 2020 |website=library.mit.edu}}</ref>

In 2010–2011, she was a fellow at the [[Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study]] at Harvard, where she investigated issues involving security of government systems, and their privacy and policy implications.<ref name=radcliffe>{{cite web |url=http://www.radcliffe.edu/fellowships/fellows_2011slandau.aspx |title=Susan Landau – Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study |publisher=Harvard University |access-date=January 9, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101127061809/http://radcliffe.edu/fellowships/fellows_2011slandau.aspx |archive-date=November 27, 2010}}</ref>

From 1999 until 2010, she specialized in [[Internet security]] at [[Sun Microsystems]].<ref name=sun>{{cite web |url=http://research.sun.com/people/slandau/ |title=Susan Landau |publisher=[[Sun Microsystems]] |access-date=September 14, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081010170032/http://research.sun.com/people/slandau |archive-date=October 10, 2008}}</ref>

In 1989, she introduced the first [[algorithm]] for deciding which [[nested radical]]s can be denested, which is known as [[Landau's algorithm]].<ref>S. Landau, "Simplification of Nested Radicals", [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|SIAM]] ''Journal of Computation'', volume 21 (1992), pages 85–110.[http://www2.computer.org/portal/web/csdl/doi/10.1109/SFCS.1989.63496]</ref>

In 1972, her project on odd [[perfect number]]s won a finalist position in the [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref name=sciam>{{cite web |url=http://www.sciam.com/article.cfm?id=susan-landau-sun-microsystems-westinghouse |title=Susan Landau: Toward Perfect Internet Security |work=Scientific American |date=September 2, 2008 |accessdate=September 14, 2008}}</ref> Outside of her technical work, she is interested in the issues of [[women in science]], maintaining the ResearcHers Email list, a "community dedicated to supporting women new to research in computing",<ref>{{cite web |title=ResearcHers Email List |url=http://systers.org/mailman/listinfo/researchers |publisher=Anita Borg Institute for Women and Technology |year=2017 |accessdate=September 11, 2017}}</ref> and an online bibliography of women's writing in computer science.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Book List: Computer Science Books by Women Computer Scientists |url=http://www.cra.org/Activities/craw/booklist/index.php |publisher=Committee on the Status of Women in Computing Research |access-date=September 14, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080915021625/http://www.cra.org/Activities/craw/booklist/index.php |archive-date=September 15, 2008}}</ref> She was awarded the 2008 [[Anita Borg Institute Women of Vision Awards|Anita Borg Institute Women of Vision Award]] for Social Impact.<ref>{{cite web |title=Women of Vision awards presented at Anita Borg Institute banquet |url=http://www.diversitycareers.com/articles/pro/08-augsep/soc_news_ABI.htm |work=Diversity/Careers |access-date=June 29, 2011 |date=August–September 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928005111/http://www.diversitycareers.com/articles/pro/08-augsep/soc_news_ABI.htm |archive-date=September 28, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=AnitaB_org |title=Susan Landau, Women of Vision Winner Social Impact |date=May 30, 2008 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JZDlsHdsj6E |accessdate=May 22, 2018}}</ref> She has been a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] since 1999,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aaas.org/fellow/landau-susan |title=AAAS Fellow / Susan Landau |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |date= |accessdate=August 27, 2017}}</ref> and in 2011 she was inducted as a [[List of Fellows of the Association for Computing Machinery|Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://fellows.acm.org/fellow_citation.cfm?id=2455723&srt=year&year=2011 |title=ACM: Fellows Award / Susan Landau |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |date= |access-date=January 1, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120722021725/http://fellows.acm.org/fellow_citation.cfm?id=2455723&srt=year&year=2011 |archive-date=July 22, 2012}}</ref> In 2012, Landau won the Surveillance Studies Network Book Prize for her book ''Surveillance or Security? The Risks Posed by New Wiretapping Technologies'', published by [[MIT Press]].  In October 2015, Landau was inducted into the [[National Cyber Security Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.techrepublic.com/article/keep-smartphones-backdoor-free-urges-cybersecurity-expert-susan-landau/ |title=Keep smartphones backdoor free, urges cybersecurity expert Susan Landau |work=Tech Republic |date=July 12, 2016 |accessdate=August 27, 2017}}</ref>

== Involvement with FBI v. Apple case ==

Landau gave testimony in the [[FBI–Apple encryption dispute]] between 2015 and 2016.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.techrepublic.com/article/keep-smartphones-backdoor-free-urges-cybersecurity-expert-susan-landau |title=Keep smartphones backdoor free, urges cybersecurity expert Susan Landau |work=Tech Republic |date=July 12, 2016 |accessdate=August 27, 2017}}</ref> She is the co-author of “Keys Under Doormats: Mandating Insecurity by Requiring Government Access to All Data and Communications,” which received the 2015 J. D. Falk Award from the Messaging Malware Mobile Anti-Abuse Working Group. The [[Obama administration]] gave substantial credit to this report's analysis when it announced that it would not pursue exceptional access to phone data.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wpi.edu/news/halloffame |title=Susan Landau, Professor of Cybersecurity Policy, to be Inducted into the Cyber Security Hall of Fame |publisher=Worcester Polytechnic Institute |date=October 26, 2015 |accessdate=August 27, 2017}}</ref>

Landau testified that making [[iPhone]]s less secure would simply send terrorists and bad actors running toward options that the FBI and Congress had no control over. Compelling Apple to weaken its software would "weaken us, but not impact the bad guys."<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.wired.com/2016/03/apple-and-fbi-iphone-hacking-fight-congressional-hearing/ |title=Apple and FBI Take Their iPhone Hacking Fight to Congress |date=March 1, 2016 |magazine=Wired}}</ref>
